title: Cache Patterns at Scale
description: Multi-level caching architectures, cache warming strategies, consistent hashing for cache clusters, and Facebook's Memcached TAO architecture.

segments.text: At Facebook-scale, a single cache layer isn't enough. They serve over 10 billion cache reads per second across a multi-level caching architecture. This lesson covers the patterns that make caching work at scale: multi-level hierarchies, warming strategies, and the legendary TAO system.

Multi-level caching follows the same principle as CPU caches. L1 is an in-process cache — a simple HashMap or Guava cache in your application. Sub-microsecond latency but limited by heap size. L2 is a distributed cache like Redis or Memcached. Sub-millisecond latency over the network. L3 is the CDN edge cache for HTTP-cacheable content.

L1 in-process caches have a consistency problem. If you have 20 application servers, each has its own L1 cache. When data changes, all 20 caches have stale data until their TTL expires. With a 30-second TTL, you serve stale data for up to 30 seconds. For user profile changes, this might be acceptable. For inventory counts during a flash sale, it's not.

Invalidation strategies for L1 caches: TTL-based is simplest but tolerates staleness. Event-driven invalidation uses Redis pub/sub or Kafka to broadcast changes to all application instances. This gives near-instant invalidation but adds infrastructure complexity. LinkedIn uses a hybrid: short TTLs plus event-driven invalidation for critical data.

You deploy a new version of your service. All 20 instances restart. Every L1 cache is empty. Every L2 cache key might have expired during deployment. Your database suddenly sees 100 percent of traffic instead of the usual 10 percent. This is the cold cache problem. How do you prevent it?
segments.thought_prompt: How would you warm caches during a rolling deployment to prevent a thundering herd on the database?

segments.text: Cache warming strategies: pre-populate from the database before the service takes traffic. Rolling deployments that keep most instances warm. Shadow traffic that replays production requests to new instances before switching. At Twitter, cache warming for their timeline service takes 30 minutes per instance — they deploy instances in waves with health checks.

When you shard a cache across multiple Redis nodes, consistent hashing determines which node stores each key. Adding or removing a node only remaps K/N keys where K is total keys and N is the number of nodes. Without it, adding one node remaps nearly all keys, causing a cache stampede. This is the same problem consistent hashing solves for any distributed data store.

Facebook's TAO is a graph-aware distributed cache built on top of Memcached and MySQL. It caches social graph relationships: friends, likes, comments. TAO handles over 10 billion reads per second with a 99.8 percent cache hit rate. The key insight: social graph queries are highly repetitive and locality-driven. Your friends list doesn't change every second.

TAO uses a leader-follower model across data centers. Writes go to the leader region's MySQL, then propagate to follower caches asynchronously. Read-after-write consistency is guaranteed within the leader region. Cross-region reads may see stale data for one to two seconds. For social graph data, this eventual consistency is perfectly acceptable.

Cache stampede, also called thundering herd: a popular key expires, and hundreds of concurrent requests all miss the cache simultaneously, all query the database, and all write back to cache. Solutions: lock-based recomputation where only one request rebuilds, probabilistic early expiration where items randomly refresh before TTL, and stale-while-revalidate patterns.

Consider this scenario at scale: your service has 10,000 unique cache keys but 3 of them account for 80 percent of reads. These hot keys all live on the same Redis shard. That shard is at CPU capacity while others idle. How do you distribute hot key load across shards without breaking cache semantics?
segments.thought_prompt: How would you handle hot keys that concentrate load on a single cache shard?

segments.text: Caching at scale is a distributed systems problem. Multi-level caches reduce latency and protect your database. Consistent hashing enables cache cluster scaling. Cache warming prevents cold-start stampedes. And hot key distribution requires deliberate engineering. Facebook processes 10 billion cache reads per second because they treat caching as a first-class architecture concern.
